r: This course builds elementary teacher candidates' capacity to analyze diverse school contexts: examining language, gender, and socioeconomic variance among students and families, auditing institutional policies for equity, and reflecting on personal attitudes that shape classroom practice. The applied tasks are synthesizing sociocultural research and writing reflective analyses of bias and equity-oriented pedagogy, which map onto O*NET training-and-teaching and information-evaluation activities that task-exposure research classifies as positively associated with writing-heavy, reasoning-heavy work. AI can already draft competent summaries of equity frameworks and diverse-learner considerations, which is genuine exposure. But the course sits inside Colorado's board-approved elementary licensure curriculum, and its instrumental purpose is professional-disposition formation candidates must personally undergo, not information a model substitutes for a person. At 24 months the licensure-curriculum constraint holds the rating down regardless of how fluently AI drafts diversity content.

By 2031, AI tutors and drafting tools will routinely generate equity analyses, diverse-learner case studies, and bias-awareness reflections, and observed-usage data already shows writing and office-style reasoning tasks as heavily used AI categories, so the knowledge-transmission portion of this course erodes further. What does not erode on this horizon is the licensure architecture: Colorado's approved elementary preparation program still requires candidates to complete this course as part of the credentialing pathway, and that mandate does not relax on a single catalog cycle. The applied work also carries a real verification dimension — a candidate's dispositions toward diverse students are assessed through supervised interaction and reflection, not through AI-graded content recall. The rating rises to Medium: the instrumental case for consuming AI-generated diversity content weakens, but the mandated course itself persists as the credentialing vehicle.

A decade out, AI is a capable and interactive explainer of equity frameworks, culturally responsive pedagogy, and sociocultural research, and the pure content-delivery rationale for this course is substantially eroded — much as it is for other introductory social-foundations survey courses. The institutional cap on F4 relaxes at ten years: accreditors and the state board could plausibly revise how dispositional and equity competencies are verified within an approved program, so the mandate is no longer certain to preserve the course in its current form. The rating holds at Medium rather than rising further, because forming a teacher candidate's own professional judgment about diverse learners is not something a model discharges on the student's behalf. The uncertainty is genuine about delivery format, not about whether some structured equity preparation remains part of licensure.
EDU 1111.d: This course is designed to increase awareness of the diverse contexts in which elementary education is situated, given our global society. Cultural and individual variances, including sociocultural factors such as language, gender, and socioeconomic status, are investigated in order to develop respect for all elementary students, families, and school communities. The course includes examining institutional policies and practices as well as personal attitudes and beliefs that influence what occurs in elementary schools. The role of the teacher/educator in equity-oriented education is explored.

r: This introductory course develops candidates' understanding of the elementary teacher's professional role: state standards, state and federal regulations, teacher-evaluation trends, and the historical, philosophical, financial, and societal foundations of schooling. The applied work is expository and analytical — researching policy contexts, writing about professional expectations, and connecting foundations content to contemporary practice — which maps to O*NET information-evaluation and training-and-teaching activities that observed-usage data shows are heavily represented in current AI use. AI already summarizes education-policy history and regulatory frameworks competently. Even so, the course is a required entry point in Colorado's board-approved elementary licensure curriculum, and the professional-identity formation it produces is not substitutable by content generation. At 24 months the rating is held down by that licensure-gated placement, not by any lack of AI capability on the content itself.

By 2031, AI will generate polished overviews of education foundations, policy trends, and evaluation frameworks on demand, and productivity research on professional writing shows AI substantially accelerating exactly this kind of expository work, so the course's information-delivery rationale continues eroding. The licensure mandate, however, changes on a multi-year accreditation cycle and is very unlikely to have been relaxed within five years — the course remains the vehicle through which Colorado's approved program certifies candidates' grounding in professional foundations. Verification also matters here in a soft sense: instructors assess candidates' developing professional judgment through discussion and applied assignments, not just factual recall AI could replicate. The rating rises to Medium, reflecting real erosion in how the content might be consumed alongside a mandate that keeps the course itself in place.

A decade out, AI explains education policy, regulatory history, and professional foundations with real sophistication, and the "learn this by reading and writing about it yourself" rationale is substantially weakened. The institutional cap loosens at this horizon: over ten years, the state board and CAEP could plausibly restructure how foundational professional knowledge is verified within an approved program, so F4's Low ceiling relaxes to Medium rather than holding firm. The rating rises to Medium accordingly — capability is high and the specific mandate is no longer certain to survive unchanged — while professional-identity formation and program gatekeeping keep it from High. The uncertainty is about pedagogical format at the ten-year horizon, not about whether some foundations requirement persists in an accredited elementary program.
EDU 2111.d: This introductory course focuses on the role of the teacher in a 21st Century classroom. Students further develop critical thinking skills to examine the realities of schools in light of contemporary trends in education. Students explore expectations of professional elementary teachers in connection to state standards, state and federal regulations, and teacher evaluation trends. Topics include teachers' current roles as instructional leaders and advocates in diverse communities as well as historical, philosophical, financial, and societal foundations in elementary education. Educational and instructional innovations in elementary education are overarching themes in the course.

r: This course examines Chicano perspectives on public education policy and contrasts learning and teaching differences among students and teachers, work that is analytical and policy-focused rather than practicum-based. The applied tasks — researching policy history, comparing pedagogical approaches, and writing critical analysis — map to O*NET information-evaluation and research activities that task-exposure research associates with AI's strengths in synthesis and writing. AI can already produce competent overviews of Chicano education history and policy debates, representing real exposure. The course description is brief, giving lower confidence in a precise task mapping, but it plausibly satisfies a diversity or multicultural competency area within the elementary program rather than being individually named by the state board, so the institutional constraint is real but softer than a clinical or board-named mandate. At 24 months the rating stays Low on capability-diffusion grounds alone.

By 2031, AI will routinely generate historical and policy analysis of Chicano education comparable to competent student work, and observed-usage data continues to show writing and research synthesis as leading AI-use categories, pushing the instrumental case for producing this analysis oneself further down. Because the course likely satisfies a broader multicultural-competency requirement rather than being the singularly board-mandated course, the institutional brake is weaker than for courses tied to clinical hours, and the softer F4 designation allows the rating to rise. Verification burden is moderate: understanding historical and structural inequities well enough to teach diverse learners still benefits from human interpretive judgment AI does not reliably supply. The rating moves to Medium, reflecting substantial erosion in the content-production rationale tempered by continuing, if less rigid, institutional expectations around diversity coursework.

A decade out, the central case has AI performing sophisticated historical and policy analysis of Chicano education and comparative pedagogy at a level competitive with much student writing, consistent with the broader trend of AI capability doubling on task-time-horizon measures every few months. The institutional requirement that elementary candidates complete some diversity- or multicultural-focused coursework plausibly persists, but which specific course satisfies it is exactly the kind of curricular detail programs revise over a decade, so the softer F4 mandate does not hold the rating at Low. The rating stays Medium: capability is high enough to substantially erode the content-generation rationale, but the interpretive, culturally grounded judgment the course cultivates in a future teacher is not something AI supplies on the student's behalf. Confidence is lower given the thin course description available.
EDU 3120.d: This course presents the Chicano perspective on current public education policy and its implementation in the schools. Examines learning and teaching differences in students and teachers.

r: This course teaches candidates to design differentiated K-6 learning environments: classroom-management and motivation strategies, technology integration, and introductory lesson planning tailored to individual student needs. The applied work blends instructional-design tasks that are moderately exposed — drafting differentiated lesson plans and technology-integration ideas, which AI already assists with — against classroom-management and motivation strategy that depends on reading real students in real time, a task-exposure category research places outside AI's current reach. The course is a required, sequenced prerequisite feeding directly into the paired instructional-assessment and field-experience courses later in the program, giving it real scaffolding weight, and it sits within Colorado's board-approved elementary licensure curriculum. At 24 months those combined constraints — foundational role plus licensure placement — hold the rating at Low even though the lesson-planning component is already meaningfully AI-assisted.

By 2031, AI lesson-plan and differentiation-strategy generators will be common classroom tools, and productivity research on AI-assisted knowledge work suggests real time savings on the instructional-design side of this course's content. But the course's foundational role — as the explicit prerequisite to the program's paired instructional-and-assessment and field-experience sequence — caps the rating at Medium only at the 24-month horizon under the framework's scaffolding rule, and the licensure mandate independently caps the rating at Low through this horizon. Classroom-management competence, the course's other core strand, remains an in-person, real-time skill that resists delegation to a model. The rating stays Low: capability growth in lesson-drafting is real, but neither the licensure placement nor the scaffolding role has loosened enough by five years to lift the ceiling.

A decade out, AI-assisted differentiation and lesson-design tools will likely be deeply embedded in teacher workflows, and the pure content-generation portion of this course's instructional-design strand is substantially eroded by then. The licensure cap on F4 relaxes at ten years, since accreditors could plausibly revise how this foundational competency is delivered within an approved program, and the course's prerequisite-scaffolding constraint no longer applies past the 24-month horizon under the framework's rule. The rating rises to Medium, reflecting real capability erosion on the planning side while classroom-management judgment — reading and motivating real children in real time — remains a genuinely human, presence-dependent skill. The uncertainty is about how much of the course shifts toward AI-tool oversight versus original design, not about whether in-person management competence stays necessary.
EDU 3222.d: This course examines features of effective K-6 learning environments and management strategies designed to facilitate learning. Practices of student motivation and discipline are covered. Students are introduced to the strategies of differentiation to enhance elementary students' individual learning that contribute to all students' success. Technology as a tool for maximizing instruction in the classroom will be integrated into course work. Lesson planning is introduced, with an emphasis on differentiating both instruction and learning environments.

r: This course teaches the relationship between differentiated instruction and assessment: modifying curriculum on the basis of individual student needs, using informal and formal assessment techniques, connecting classroom assessment to district and state mandated testing, and communicating professionally about assessment and instruction — work performed concurrently with the paired 45-hour field placement. The applied tasks map to O*NET evaluating-information and communicating-with-others activities, and while AI already drafts assessment items and analyzes score data competently, the course's tight coupling to live field practice with real elementary students keeps the embodied, real-time application dimension protective. It is also the explicit prerequisite for the program's science, health, and mathematics methods courses, giving it strong foundational weight, and it sits inside Colorado's board-approved licensure curriculum. At 24 months these combined constraints hold the rating at Low despite substantial AI capability on assessment-item generation itself.

By 2031, AI-assisted assessment analytics — flagging performance patterns, drafting formative items, summarizing data for instructional decisions — will be common in classrooms, and observed-usage data already shows this kind of structured analytical work as a leading AI-use category, eroding the course's execution rationale. What holds the rating at Low through this horizon is the combination of the course's role as prerequisite substrate for three later required methods courses and its placement within the state's approved licensure sequence, both of which the framework treats as hard ceilings that do not lift within one or two catalog cycles. Professional communication about a real child's assessment data also carries real verification stakes that keep expert judgment in the loop. The rating stays Low, reflecting a case where strong capability growth is real but structurally capped rather than realized in the instrumental need.

A decade out, AI performs assessment-data analysis and instructional-modification recommendations at a high level, and the execution rationale for this course's applied tasks is substantially eroded by then, consistent with the broader trajectory of capability growth in analytical and writing-adjacent work. Both structural ceilings loosen somewhat at ten years: the foundational-scaffolding cap and the licensure cap each explicitly relax to Medium at this horizon under the framework's rule, since accreditors could plausibly redesign how assessment competency is built and verified across a decade. The rating rises to Medium accordingly, while the course's function of certifying a candidate's judgment about real children's assessment data — not a model's — keeps it from reaching High. The uncertainty is substantial about how the methods sequence restructures around AI assessment tools, not about whether that judgment stays necessary.
EDU 3444.d: This course is designed to assist teacher candidates in understanding the important relationship between effective instructional practice and assessment in the differentiated elementary classroom. Modifications of curriculum and instruction are emphasized on the basis of individual student interests, strengths and needs. Informal and formal assessment techniques are examined along with the commonalities between classroom assessments and larger scale local, district and state mandated assessments. Emphasis is placed upon collecting and utilizing assessment data to drive instruction in differentiated classrooms. Professional communication regarding assessment and instruction is also a focus of this course.

r: This field experience requires 45 hours of supervised work in an assigned elementary classroom, assisting the teacher and implementing differentiated instruction and assessment, including teaching multiple small-group and whole-class lessons. The applied activity is in-person instructional delivery and real-time interpersonal judgment with elementary-age minors — squarely in the low-exposure, high-presence categories task-exposure research places outside AI's current reach. The binding constraint is a hard institutional lock: Colorado educator licensure conditions completion of an approved preparation program that logs mandated field hours, layered with CAEP clinical-practice expectations, and none of those hours can be satisfied by an AI system standing in for the candidate. At 24 months the instrumental need for supervised classroom teaching experience is fully intact; capability growth elsewhere in AI is simply not the operative variable for this course's requirement.

AI will increasingly assist classroom teachers with assessment design and data analysis by 2031, and that augmentation will be visible in the placement classrooms candidates work in. But this field experience exists to develop a candidate's own embodied competence teaching and assessing live learners under supervision, a formative, presence-dependent activity automation does not perform on the student's behalf. Verification burden is real given child-welfare stakes, keeping a knowledgeable supervising teacher and instructor in the loop rather than an automated substitute. The Colorado licensure field-hour mandate does not relax within a catalog cycle or two, and CAEP's clinical-practice expectations reinforce it. The instrumental case is preserved by embodiment and institutional lock-in acting together; AI changes what candidates observe and use in placement classrooms, not whether they must personally log the supervised hours.

Even under a decade of substantial capability growth and broad classroom-AI diffusion, the requirement that teacher candidates personally accumulate supervised in-person field hours with elementary students is among the most durable constraints in the catalog, and there is no credible central-case path to its removal by 2036. The embodied, interpersonal nature of small-group and whole-class teaching resists direct substitution regardless of how sophisticated instructional-support tools become. The genuine uncertainty concerns what candidates are assessing and how heavily AI mediates the instruction they observe and assist with — not whether the field-hour requirement itself, and the human competence it certifies, remains necessary. The rating holds Low with high confidence, anchored by the licensure mandate and the embodied character of the work rather than by any assumption about AI's ceiling.
EDU 3445.d: This field experience, as a partner with EDU 3444, requires 45 hours of field work in an assigned elementary school. Field work involves assisting the classroom teacher and implementing appropriate classroom instruction and assessment. Teaching multiple small group and whole class lessons is a focus of this experience. Assessments data is used to inform instructional design and implantation of lessons.

r: This survey course covers the history, myths, and characteristics of gifted and talented learners, identification procedures and service models, and teaching and learning models for appropriate curriculum design. The applied work is expository and design-oriented — synthesizing research on giftedness and drafting curriculum and service-model frameworks — which maps to O*NET information-evaluation and training-and-teaching activities that observed-usage data shows are heavily represented in current AI use for writing and analytical tasks. AI can already summarize identification criteria and generate differentiated curriculum ideas for gifted learners competently. The course likely satisfies a specialized competency area within the elementary program rather than being the singular state-board-named requirement, so its institutional lock is real but softer than a clinical-hours mandate. At 24 months the rating stays Low primarily on adoption-lag grounds rather than deep structural protection.

By 2031, AI-assisted identification screening support and curriculum-design tools for gifted learners will plausibly be in broader use, and productivity research on professional writing and content generation suggests real efficiency gains on the course's expository and design-oriented tasks. Because the F4 designation here is the softer strong-mandate tier rather than a hard course-specific lock, the ceiling relaxes earlier than it would for a licensure-clinical course, allowing the rating to rise once base capability crosses the framework's threshold. Verification still matters: misidentifying or mis-serving gifted learners has real consequences for students, keeping expert judgment relevant even as AI drafts more of the supporting material. The rating moves to Medium, reflecting genuine capability erosion in the course's knowledge-delivery function balanced against continued, if not rigidly mandated, professional relevance.

A decade out, AI explains giftedness theory, identification frameworks, and service-model design with real sophistication, consistent with the broader capability trend of rapid growth in task-time-horizon performance, and the pure content-delivery rationale for this course is substantially eroded. The softer institutional constraint here does not tighten back up over time, so the rating does not fall, but the course's role in cultivating a candidate's own judgment about identifying and serving a specific, sometimes overlooked student population is not something AI discharges on the candidate's behalf. The rating holds at Medium: capability is high and the specific-course mandate is not a hard lock, yet professional judgment about real students keeps it from High. The uncertainty is genuine about how the specialization is taught under ubiquitous AI content tools, not about whether it persists in some form.
EDU 3460.d: This class focuses on the history, myths, and characteristics of gifted and talented students as learners. It presents procedures for identification and service models, as well as teaching and learning models for appropriate curriculum.

r: This methods course teaches candidates to plan K-6 science and health instruction, using assessment data to guide instruction for diverse learners, with emphasis on hands-on, inquiry-based experiences and critical-thinking, problem-solving skills — implemented concurrently in the paired 45-hour field placement. The applied tasks blend instructional-design work that is moderately exposed, such as drafting hands-on lesson sequences AI can already assist with, against the embodied, real-time delivery of active science and health lessons to real elementary students, a category task-exposure research places outside AI's reach. The course sits within Colorado's board-approved licensure curriculum and is tightly coupled to concurrent field practice, keeping the embodiment dampener active. At 24 months the rating is Low: capability on the planning side is real, but the field-linked delivery component and licensure placement together hold the applied need firmly in place.

By 2031, AI-assisted science and health lesson-planning tools, including differentiated activity generation and assessment-data analysis, will be common, and observed-usage data already shows this kind of structured analytical drafting as a leading AI-use category, eroding the planning-side rationale further. What keeps the rating at Low through this horizon is the course's continued pairing with live field placement — hands-on inquiry lessons must still be delivered to real children by the candidate — and its position inside the state's approved licensure sequence, a constraint that does not relax within a catalog cycle or two. The dampening effect of that embodied, field-coupled delivery, combined with the licensure ceiling, outweighs the real gains AI provides on the preparatory side. The rating stays Low, reflecting strong capability growth that has not yet reached the operative, in-person instructional task.

A decade out, AI performs sophisticated science and health lesson design and assessment-data analysis, and the planning-side execution rationale is substantially eroded by then, in line with the broader trajectory of rapid capability growth. The licensure cap on F4 explicitly relaxes to Medium at the ten-year horizon under the framework's rule, since accreditors could plausibly revise how methods competency is verified within an approved program over a decade. The rating rises to Medium accordingly, while the hands-on, real-time delivery of inquiry-based lessons to actual elementary students — the course's other core strand — remains genuinely embodied and resistant to substitution. The uncertainty is substantial about how heavily AI mediates lesson preparation by 2036, not about whether a candidate must still personally lead the hands-on classroom experience.
EDU 3550.d: This course focuses on teaching science and health to K-6 students, with an emphasis on concepts and processes, and the methods pertinent to the construction of elementary science and health content. This course provides the opportunity to use assessment data to guide science and health instruction to meet the needs of diverse learners. Emphasis is placed on critical thinking, problem solving and decision making skills by exploring these ideas through hands-on experiences. Development of positive attitudes towards science and health is examined. Teacher candidates implement these instructional practices in the co-requisite field experience.

r: This field experience, paired with the science-health and mathematics methods courses, requires 45 hours of supervised work in an assigned elementary school, teaching multiple small-group and whole-class lessons that implement differentiated, hands-on instructional practices with discourse-based concept-building, using collected data to inform instruction. The applied activity is in-person instructional delivery and real-time interpersonal judgment with elementary-age minors, a category task-exposure research places among the least automatable. The binding constraint is a hard institutional lock: Colorado teacher-licensure preparation requires substantial supervised field hours that a board must approve as part of the program, and CAEP clinical-practice expectations reinforce it — none of these hours can be logged by an AI system standing in for the candidate. At 24 months the instrumental need for this supervised teaching experience is fully intact regardless of AI's capability elsewhere.

AI-assisted lesson-planning and data-analysis tools will be more visible in the placement classrooms candidates work in by 2031, but this field experience exists specifically to build a candidate's own embodied teaching competence — leading hands-on, discourse-rich lessons and managing real learners under supervision — a formative, presence-dependent activity automation does not perform on the candidate's behalf. Verification burden is real given the stakes of working with children, keeping a supervising teacher and program instructor in the loop rather than an automated proxy. The Colorado field-hour mandate and CAEP clinical-practice expectations do not relax within a catalog cycle or two. The instrumental case is preserved jointly by embodiment and institutional lock-in; AI changes the tools candidates observe in placement classrooms, not whether they must personally accumulate the supervised hours themselves.

Even a decade of substantial capability growth and wide classroom-AI diffusion does not plausibly reach the requirement that teacher candidates personally log supervised in-person field hours delivering hands-on, discourse-based lessons to elementary students — among the most durable constraints in the catalog, with no credible central-case path to removal by 2036. The embodied, interpersonal, real-time nature of small-group and whole-class teaching resists direct substitution no matter how capable instructional-support software becomes. Genuine uncertainty concerns how heavily AI mediates the content and data candidates work with in placement classrooms, not whether the field-hour requirement itself, and the human competence it certifies, remains necessary. The rating holds Low with high confidence, anchored by the licensure mandate and the embodied character of hands-on elementary teaching rather than by any assumption about AI's future ceiling.
EDU 3665.d: This field experience, paired with EDU 3550 and EDU 3666, requires 45 hours of field experience at an assigned elementary school. This field work includes teaching multiple small group and whole class lessons while implementing differentiated instructional practices in mathematics, science, and/or health. Emphasis is placed on active, hands-on lessons with discourse to facilitate constructing concepts. Data collection and analysis informs instruction.

r: This methods course teaches candidates to plan K-6 mathematics instruction from academic standards and student needs, emphasizing problem solving, mathematical reasoning, and discourse, with formative and summative assessment data guiding instruction — implemented concurrently in the paired field placement. Mathematical content generation and problem-set design are areas task-exposure research flags among the most AI-exposed, since quantitative and computational reasoning ranks among the categories most associated with automation, so the planning-side tasks here are meaningfully exposed already. What keeps the applied need in place is the embodied delivery strand: leading real-time discourse and reasoning-focused lessons with elementary students in the concurrent field placement, plus the course's position inside Colorado's board-approved licensure curriculum. At 24 months the rating is Low, held there by field-coupled delivery and licensure placement despite real exposure on the math-content side.

By 2031, AI math-problem generation, adaptive practice design, and assessment-data analysis will be routine classroom tools, and task-exposure research's association of quantitative and computational work with high exposure continues pushing the planning-side rationale down. But the course remains tightly coupled to concurrent field practice — candidates must still lead real discourse-based mathematical reasoning lessons with actual children — and the licensure ceiling on this required, board-approved course does not relax within a catalog cycle or two. The dampening effect of that embodied, real-time delivery component, layered onto the licensure cap, keeps the rating at Low even though the underlying mathematical content is now substantially AI-generable. The rating reflects a course where capability growth on the knowledge side outpaces the structural constraints holding the applied requirement in place.

A decade out, AI generates and adapts K-6 mathematics content, problem sets, and assessment analytics at a high level, consistent with quantitative reasoning's position among the more AI-exposed task categories and the broader trend of rapid capability growth. The licensure cap on F4 relaxes to Medium at the ten-year horizon under the framework's rule, since accreditors could plausibly revise how mathematics-methods competency is delivered and verified within an approved program over a decade. The rating rises to Medium accordingly, while leading real-time, discourse-based mathematical reasoning instruction with actual elementary students — the course's embodied core — remains resistant to substitution. The uncertainty is substantial about how much AI mediates lesson content and practice design by 2036, not about whether a candidate must still personally lead that classroom discourse.
EDU 3666.d: Teacher candidates apply appropriate academic standards and knowledge of K-6 student needs to plan evidence- based, mathematics instruction for diverse learners. Knowledge of K- 6 mathematics concepts are applied to lessons designed to increase student achievement through stimulating problem solving, mathematical reasoning, and discourse. Formative and summative assessment data are utilized to plan instruction. Teacher candidates implement these practices in the co-requisite field experience.

r: This course places teacher candidates in British classrooms for direct field hours alongside comparative analysis of Colorado and United Kingdom educational philosophies, methods, and outcomes. The applied work is twofold: in-person observation and participation in a live foreign classroom, plus written comparison of curricular and cultural approaches. Task-exposure research classifies comparative-writing tasks as considerably more exposed than the embodied fieldwork itself, which sits in the low-exposure, high-presence category requiring real-time interpersonal judgment with children and cooperating teachers abroad. The binding constraint is the course's supervised field-hours structure, contributory to the broader teacher-preparation field-experience total even though this particular study-abroad option is not itself a hard licensure mandate. At 24 months, with essentially no diffusion of AI into international field placements, the instrumental need to complete firsthand classroom observation abroad stays fully intact.

By 2031, AI translation and research tools will make the comparative-analysis paper easier to draft, and observed-usage data already shows writing and synthesis tasks as a prominent AI-use category, pushing that portion of the coursework toward automatability. What survives is the embodied requirement itself: a candidate physically present in a British school, observing real students and a real cooperating teacher, cannot be substituted by a model. Verification of what was actually seen and how it compares to Colorado practice still depends on the student's own presence and judgment. The field-hours contribution to teacher-preparation totals persists across a catalog cycle. The rating holds Low: the writing artifact automates, but the instrumental purpose of the course, direct comparative field experience, does not.

A decade out, AI could plausibly generate sophisticated comparative-education analysis from published sources without a student ever leaving Colorado, and the honest uncertainty is whether virtual or AI-mediated cross-cultural exposure substitutes for physical travel in some students' eyes. But the central case still requires the embodied act, being in a British classroom, to certify the comparative field experience this course is built around, and nothing in the capability trajectory removes the value of firsthand presence for interpersonal, real-time observation of another country's teaching practice. The rating stays Low, held by embodiment rather than by a hard institutional mandate. The genuine caveat is that the balance between physical and virtual cultural exchange is the most plausible axis of change, not whether direct field presence remains the point.
EDU 3700.d: This course focuses on first hand experiences with culture and the education system in Great Britain. Students will complete field hours in schools in Great Britain and participate in cultural experiences. The focus of the course will be to compare and contrast cultural beliefs and educational philosophies, methods, and outcomes of Great Britain to Colorado.

r: The course analyzes historical and contemporary factors shaping the education of African American children and develops the knowledge, skills, and dispositions educators need to teach equitably, integrating theoretical research with practical application toward reflective decision-making. The applied work is critical historical analysis, discussion, and disposition-building rather than fieldwork with children, so task-exposure research's finding that critical-thinking-intensive work is comparatively low-exposure applies, even as the writing components are more automatable. The binding constraint is verification burden: AI-generated guidance on educating a specific, historically marginalized population risks reproducing stereotype or superficial framing, so an instructor and reflective learner must check it against lived and scholarly context. At 24 months, with negligible classroom diffusion of AI into equity-focused teacher preparation, the instrumental need to build this disposition-forming competence directly is essentially unchanged.

By 2031, AI will fluently generate historical synthesis and discussion prompts about African American educational history, eroding the "produce the analysis yourself" rationale for much of the written coursework. But the jagged-frontier problem is acute here: a plausible-sounding AI account of culturally responsive practice can be confidently wrong in ways that are not obvious to someone without the grounding the course provides, so verification burden keeps a knowledgeable human central. The course carries no hard licensure clock, but it functions as a required component within the School of Education's accredited preparation sequence, which does not restructure within a catalog cycle. The rating rises to Medium: content delivery increasingly automates, while the disposition and judgment the course is meant to instill remain the harder-to-substitute residue.

A decade out, AI will be a fluent and well-read interlocutor on the history and pedagogy of educating African American children, and the pure information-delivery rationale for the course is substantially eroded. What plausibly remains load-bearing is the reflective, dispositional competence, the capacity to recognize when an AI-generated recommendation is culturally tone-deaf, historically thin, or built on an unrepresentative training corpus, which is precisely a verification skill rather than an information-retrieval one, and one the course is specifically designed to instill through guided reflection rather than content transmission alone. The course's place inside the accredited teacher-preparation sequence is likely to persist in the central case, though its instructional format could shift markedly toward guided critique of AI-generated pedagogical material. The rating holds Medium; the uncertainty concerns pedagogy under ubiquitous AI, not whether the underlying equity competence remains instrumentally necessary for future educators serving this population.
EDU 4010.d: This course analyzes the historical and contemporary factors that influence the education of African American children in the United States. Focus is on the knowledge, skills, and dispositions required by educational institutions, educators, and parents to provide an effective and equitable education for African American children. Practical application is integrated with theoretical research and conceptual information. Students who successfully complete this course will receive introductory skills and experiences as effective practitioners, reflective decision makers, and resources for the community.

r: This methods course teaches concepts and instructional practices for elementary social studies, covering history, geography, civics, and economics, and culminates in a candidate-designed inquiry learning experience that applies pedagogical content knowledge and literacy scaffolding. The applied task, drafting lesson sequences and instructional materials, sits in a moderately exposed band; AI curriculum-generation tools already draft passable social-studies units, but developmentally appropriate sequencing for real elementary learners still needs expert judgment. The binding constraint is that this content-area methods course is a required component of the CAEP- and Colorado-accredited elementary licensure pathway, feeding directly into the supervised residencies that follow it. At 24 months, with minimal classroom diffusion of AI curriculum tools and full licensure-sequence intactness, the instrumental need to build this instructional-design competence firsthand remains essentially unchanged.

By 2031, AI lesson-planning and curriculum-generation tools will handle much of the routine drafting this course currently teaches by hand, meaningfully eroding the "design it yourself" rationale for producing inquiry units. Observed-usage data already shows writing and planning tasks as a large and growing AI-use category, reinforcing that trend. What resists automation is the pedagogical judgment needed to verify that an AI-drafted unit is developmentally appropriate and integrates disciplinary thinking correctly for young learners, a real verification burden. The course's status inside the accredited licensure sequence, which does not restructure on a five-year clock, keeps it required regardless of how automatable draft generation becomes. The rating stays Low, tracking the binding accreditation constraint even as the underlying design task becomes AI-deliverable.

A decade out, the central case has AI generating strong first-draft social-studies units routinely, and the execution rationale for teaching candidates to build units from scratch is substantially eroded. Here the institutional cap plausibly relaxes: over ten years accreditors and the state licensure board could revise how content-area methods competency is demonstrated, no longer requiring the same course structure. The rating rises to Medium, reflecting that the applied design task is highly automatable and the mandate is not certain to hold the course unchanged, while the residual instructional-judgment and inquiry-design competence, plus the possibility of a continued mandate, keep it from High. The Low-Low-Medium trajectory mirrors other licensure-adjacent methods courses where capability outruns the accreditation clock only at the long horizon.
EDU 4011.d: This course focuses on concepts and instructional practices for teaching elementary social studies in powerful and purposeful ways. This includes methods for teaching history, geography, civics, and economics within a multicultural, global society. In addition, this course will explore the integrative nature of the social studies with an emphasis on disciplinary content, thinking, and literacy. These practices will be applied to the development of an inquiry learning experience that engages students in a series of curricular decisions that focus on instructional methods and their use in developing disciplinary content, thinking, and literacy-scaffolding pre-service teachers' knowledge development of powerful and purposeful methods for teaching the social studies.

r: Residency I is a clinical placement requiring at least three full instructional days weekly in an assigned elementary classroom, synthesizing prior coursework into professionalism, instructional design, assessment, motivation, and family collaboration under close mentor supervision. The applied work is direct, embodied classroom practice: observing, co-teaching, and eventually independently leading real children through real lessons, activities that task-exposure research places firmly outside AI's automatable range. The binding constraint is absolute: Colorado educator licensure and CAEP clinical-practice expectations require this supervised field placement with its own clock hours, and no AI system performs supervised teaching practice on a candidate's behalf. At 24 months the instrumental need for this embodied residency is completely untouched; capability growth in lesson-planning tools is simply not the operative variable for a course defined by supervised presence in a classroom.

By 2031, AI will meaningfully assist mentor and resident teachers with lesson drafting, data analysis, and administrative documentation inside the placement classroom, and that augmentation will be visible in the residency itself, likely reshaping how much clerical work fills a resident's day. But Residency I exists to certify a candidate's embodied competence managing, teaching, and being accountable for real learners under close supervision, a formative, presence-dependent activity that automation does not perform on the student's behalf regardless of how capable the drafting tools become. Child-welfare stakes keep verification burden high, and the Colorado licensure clinical-hours requirement does not loosen within a single catalog-revision cycle. The rating stays Low: AI reshapes what the resident learns to use and oversee inside the classroom, not whether the resident must physically be there accumulating supervised instructional responsibility.

Even under a decade of rapid capability growth and broad classroom AI adoption, the requirement that teacher candidates accumulate substantial, sequential, supervised classroom days before advancing to the culminating residency is among the most durable constraints in the education catalog, and there is no credible central-case path to its removal by 2036 absent a fundamental restructuring of how Colorado licenses teachers. The embodied, real-time, interpersonal nature of managing a classroom of children resists direct substitution regardless of how capable instructional-support tools become. The genuine uncertainty concerns how heavily AI mediates lesson preparation and assessment inside the placement, not whether the supervised-presence requirement itself persists. The rating holds Low with high confidence, anchored by the same licensure and embodiment logic that protects other clinical-practice courses in this catalog.
EDU 4115.d: This clinical residency requires at least three full, sequential instructional days per week in an assigned accredited public or private elementary classroom. The residency and accompanying seminar include opportunities to synthesize content from all previous coursework, including: professionalism; designing, implementing, and assessing instruction; student motivation and engagement; and collaboration with colleagues and families. The teacher candidate is an active participant in the elementary school community through close observation of the mentor teacher, collaborative practice with the mentor teacher, and/or supervised independent practice. Concepts and skills learned in RDG 4444 are a particular focus in this residency; however, the resident engages in all content areas.

A decade out, AI translation and cross-linguistic communication tools will be considerably more capable and embedded in classrooms serving English learners, plausibly easing some family-communication and material-adaptation burden that currently falls to the resident and cooperating teacher. But the CLD Residency's core purpose, certifying a candidate's embodied, supervised competence teaching and building relationships with linguistically diverse students and families, is not a task AI performs for the student, and Colorado's licensure and endorsement architecture shows no credible path to removing the supervised-hours requirement by 2036. The uncertainty is genuinely about how much of the language-support work automates around the resident, not about whether the supervised placement itself remains necessary. EDU 4116.d: This clinical residency in a classroom with culturally and linguistically diverse (CLD) learners requires at least three full, sequential instructional days per week in an assigned accredited public or private elementary classroom with English Language Learners. The CLD residency and accompanying seminar includes opportunities to synthesize content from all previous coursework, including concentration coursework for serving CLD students: methods for teaching CLD learners; professionalism; designing, implementing, and assessing instruction for diverse learners; student motivation and engagement; and collaboration with colleagues and families, particularly diverse families. The teacher candidate is an active participant in the elementary school community through close observation of the mentor teacher, collaborative practice with the mentor teacher, and/or supervised independent practice. Concepts and skills learned in RDG 4444 are a particular focus in this residency; however, residents are engaged in all content areas.

EDU 4190.d: This is a supervised, full-time field experience in an accredited public or private elementary school, providing increasing responsibility for the teaching, supervision, and assessment of learners (grades K-6). Ten hours of seminar are required (five hours for six credit course). To pass this course, and be recommended for licensure, teacher candidates must be minimally rated as proficient in all Performance-Based Standards for Colorado Teachers. Each student teacher is required to complete the Teacher Work Sample with all requirements rates as proficient or higher.

r: Designing Instruction for All Learners teaches data-literate teaching: selecting and creating valid assessments, analyzing resultant data, and planning differentiated instruction with grouping and classroom-management strategies, applied concurrently in the co-requisite Residency II placement. The applied work, assessment design and data analysis, sits closer to the more-exposed end of teaching tasks; AI already drafts assessment items and summarizes performance data competently, a business-and-financial-adjacent analytical activity observed-usage data shows growing AI use around. But misreading a student's assessment data and misdirecting a differentiation plan has real instructional consequences, and the course's tight coupling to the mandatory Residency II placement folds it into the same accredited licensure sequence. At 24 months the instrumental need to build this analytical competence directly, rather than delegate it, remains largely intact.

By 2031, AI assessment-analytics tools will competently flag performance patterns, suggest groupings, and draft differentiated materials, substantially automating the execution this course currently teaches candidates to do by hand. The residue is verification: catching when an AI-suggested grouping or intervention misreads a specific student's actual need, a real error-cost concern given the diverse learners the course addresses by name and the diverse classroom in which the candidate concurrently practices. Because the course is a co-requisite of the mandated clinical residency and sits inside the same accredited licensure sequence, that structural requirement does not relax within a catalog cycle even as the underlying analytical tasks become AI-deliverable. The rating stays Low: the residency-coupling constraint dominates near-term, even as the data-literacy tasks it teaches grow substantially more automatable.

A decade out, AI-driven assessment analytics and differentiation planning will likely be routine in classrooms, and the "analyze and plan it yourself" rationale for this course's content is substantially eroded relative to how it is taught today. The institutional coupling to Residency II plausibly loosens over ten years as accreditors reconsider how data-literacy competency is demonstrated within a restructured practicum sequence. The rating rises to Medium, reflecting that the applied analytical tasks are highly automatable and the current course-and-residency pairing is not certain to persist unchanged, while the residual judgment needed to verify AI-generated instructional recommendations for real, individual students keeps it from reaching High. This Low-Low-Medium trajectory mirrors other licensure-coupled analytical courses in this catalog where capability advances faster than the accreditation structure surrounding them.
EDU 4222.d: This course focuses on the knowledge and skills of data literate teachers, who can select and create valid and reliable assessments, critically analyze resultant assessment data, and plan instruction utilizing varied differentiation models to increase academic achievement for students with diverse learning needs. Attention is given to grouping strategies and management of the classroom environment for successful whole group, small group and individual instruction. Tracking individual and class performance through multiple measures and analyzing the success of differentiated instructional sequences is included. Teacher candidates apply these techniques in the co-requisite Residency II and reflect upon successes, challenges, and adaptations in practice with course peers.

EDU 4225.d: This culminating, full-time clinical residency will place the teacher candidate in an assigned, accredited public or private elementary school. Close collaboration between the candidate and mentor teacher will occur in a variety of ways, including the candidate taking the role of lead teacher. The candidate will assume responsibility for all functions of the classroom, including overall design and implementation of instruction and assessment in all curricular areas, maintenance of a productive classroom environment tailored to the needs of diverse learners, communication with colleagues and families, and integration of technology to improve student learning. Knowledge and skills gained in the corequisite EDU 4222 course concerning assessment, data, and use of specific instructional strategies for identified needs are practiced, and the teacher candidates evaluate these practices in light of class and individual academic achievement. Seminar accompanies Residency II.

EDU 4590.d: Satisfaction of all student teaching application requirements by the required deadline. Passage of the Linguistically Diverse PLACE test. Corequisite: In addition to taking EDU 4590 students must complete eight weeks of student teaching (EDU 4190, EDS 4290, or ECE 4390) in an elementary, secondary, or early childhood classroom working with a cooperating teacher in their initial licensure area. This course is a supervised, full-time, eight- week student-teaching experience in an accredited public or private school's linguistically diverse program. The experience provides increasing responsibility for the teaching, supervising, and directing of an identified group of English language learners, K-12. Teacher candidates must attend 10 hours of seminar conducted by college supervisors of student teaching. For this course, teacher candidates work with a linguistically diverse teacher and demonstrate proficiency in all phases of linguistically diverse classroom instruction. Teacher candidates are required to complete components of the teacher work sample and demonstrate proficiency in Performance Based Standards for Colorado Teachers as well as Colorado Linguistically Diverse Endorsement Standards. Proficiency required for recommendation for linguistically diverse endorsement includes ability to impact English language learners' academic success and to develop their English language proficiency.

r: The applied work is substitute teaching in elementary and middle school classrooms: managing student behavior, supervising minors, delivering the absent teacher's lesson plans, and exercising real-time interpersonal judgment in a room full of children. These map to O*NET activities like Training and Teaching Others, Assisting and Caring for Others, and Performing for or Working Directly with the Public, categories task-exposure research consistently classifies as low-exposure, since manual, physical, and caring work sits well outside AI's reach. A model can draft a worksheet or a warm-up activity, but it cannot stand in front of children, maintain order, or keep them safe. The binding constraint is embodiment: substitute instruction is definitionally in-person and presence-dependent, and no available AI capability performs it. At 24 months the instrumental need for a workshop building classroom-management confidence and technique is untouched; capability in adjacent artifact generation is simply not the operative variable here.

By 2031, AI will more capably assist substitutes with lesson materials, differentiated worksheets, item generation, and quick activity ideas, and such tools will be common in classrooms. That augments preparation; it does not supervise a class of children, de-escalate a conflict, or respond to a live behavioral situation. Child-welfare and safety stakes make the verification burden real, since errors carry non-obvious, high-cost consequences, so a knowledgeable adult must remain physically in the room. Diffusion evidence reinforces the point: Census BTOS shows only about 18% of firms using AI at end-2025, adoption lagging capability, and classroom staffing does not restructure on this horizon. There is no hard course-specific licensure lock on this particular workshop, but embodiment does the protective work because the target role is irreducibly in-person. The instrumental case is preserved by presence-dependence and verification burden together; AI changes what a substitute can prepare, not whether a human must be present.

Even under a decade of aggressive capability growth and broad classroom AI adoption, the core of substitute teaching, embodied supervision of minors, real-time behavior management, and in-person instruction delivery, resists direct substitution, because it sits at the intersection of the lowest-exposure task categories: physical presence and interpersonal caring. The genuine uncertainty is how heavily AI mediates the instructional content a substitute delivers and how much material generation shifts to models, which is the honest ten-year hedge here. But no central-case path removes the need for a competent human adult physically present with children by 2036, and this workshop exists to build exactly that in-person competence and confidence. Base automatability ticks up only modestly as artifact generation matures, yet embodiment holds the rating at Low. The instrumental necessity of learning to manage and supervise a live classroom endures even as the tools a substitute carries into it change.
EDU 4700.d: This course provides the background knowledge, methods, techniques and materials for substitute teachers at the elementary and middle school levels to be more confident and competent substitute instructors. English
